title: Drugging the Undruggable: Benchmarking and Modeling Fragment-Based Screening
claim: Important targets have shallow pockets where standard screening fails, but fragments can be linked into potent compounds, and our benchmark covers this harder regime.
layout: 3 panels: a top-left 3-step flow, a right violin plot, a bottom row of violins
description: The figure has three parts. Panel (a), across the top left, shows three 3D protein-surface renderings joined by blue arrows. The first is an undruggable BCL-xL pocket. The second has two green fragments (Frag-1 and Frag-2), circled in green and red and labeled with weak Ki values in µM. The third shows the linked Compound-1 with a Ki of 36 nM. Dotted green and red arrows trace each fragment into the final molecule. Panel (b), at the top right, is a violin plot of Glide EF@1% on DUD-E. Dashed lines mark Glide on DUD-E at 16.18, Glide on FragBench at 1.82 and Random at 1.00. Panel (c), along the bottom, has four violin plots of pocket properties (SiteScore, Dscore, contact, size). Each compares FragBench in blue with DEKOIS, DUD-E and LIT-PCBA, and reports Mann–Whitney U p-values and Cliff's δ. The eye goes first to the colorful molecular renderings.
caption: (a) Fragment-based drug discovery on BCL-xL, a shallow-pocket undruggable target where conventional screening fails. Weakly binding fragments identified by NMR were linked to yield compound-1 with markedly improved affinity. (b) Glide (Halgren et al., 2004) shows poor enrichment on such targets (EF1 = 1.8), barely above random. (c) Pocket property distributions of FragBench (green) versus DUD-E (purple), with significance tested by Mann–Whitney U and effect sizes reported as Cliff’s δ.
abstract: A significant portion of disease-relevant proteins remain undruggable due to shallow, flexible, or otherwise ill-defined binding pockets that hinder conventional molecule screening. Fragment-based drug discovery (FBDD) offers a promising alternative, as small, low-complexity fragments can flexibly engage shallow, transient, or cryptic binding pockets that are often inaccessible to conventional drug-like molecules. However, fragment screening remains difficult due to weak binding signals, limited experimental throughput, and a lack of computational tools tailored for this setting. In this work, we introduce FragBench, the first benchmark for fragment-level virtual screening on undruggable targets. We construct a high-quality dataset through multi-agent LLM–human collaboration and interaction-based fragment labeling. To address the core modeling challenge, we propose a novel tri-modal contrastive learning framework FragCLIP that jointly encodes fragments, full molecules, and protein pockets. Our method significantly outperforms baselines like docking software and other ML based methods. Moreover, we demonstrate that retrieved fragments can be effectively expanded or linked into larger compounds with improved predicted binding affinity, supporting their utility as viable starting points for drug design.
